decks.title: The Harappan Civilisation — Part 1: Sources, Structures and Seals
goals: Place the Harappan Civilisation in time and space and name the main sites
Describe the Great Bath, the Citadel, the dockyard at Lothal and the granaries, and what they tell us
Explain the importance of seals, the bearded man and the bronze figure of a young woman
Explain why the undeciphered script limits our knowledge and why interpretations must be weighed

slides.heading: The Harappan Civilisation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a **city civilisation** known mainly from what its people left in the ground.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: where and when the civilisation flourished, the great structures, the seals, figures and script, and how historians read the evidence
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: More than four thousand years ago, cities with straight streets and covered drains flourished in the Indus region. We cannot read their writing, so we learn about them from the ruins and objects they left behind. In this part we study the great structures, the seals and statues, and how historians read such evidence carefully.

slides.narration: The mature phase of the Harappan Civilisation is dated to about twenty six hundred to nineteen hundred before the Common Era. Some books give about twenty five hundred to seventeen fifty. Scholars differ, so we say about. The cities were dug up only in the nineteen twenties, first at Harappa in nineteen twenty one and then at Mohenjo-daro in nineteen twenty two.

slides.heading: Where were the cities?
slides.body_md: The civilisation spread across today's Pakistan and north-western India.

slides.narration: This sketch shows some Harappan sites. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are in present-day Pakistan. Lothal and Dholavira are in Gujarat, Kalibangan is in Rajasthan, and Rakhigarhi and Banawali are in Haryana. Ropar is in Punjab. Remember that the map is a schematic sketch, not drawn to scale, and the positions are only approximate.

slides.heading: Discovery and names
bullets: **Harappa** dug from **1921** (Daya Ram Sahni); **Mohenjo-daro** from **1922** (R. D. Banerji).
John Marshall directed the **Archaeological Survey**.
Called the **Harappan** or **Indus** civilisation; some books say Indus-Saraswati.

visual.alt: Table of the two first great excavations: Harappa in Punjab, Pakistan, from 1921 under Daya Ram Sahni, and Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, Pakistan, from 1922 under R. D. Banerji; John Marshall directed the Archaeological Survey

slides.narration: Excavations at Harappa began in nineteen twenty one under Daya Ram Sahni, and at Mohenjo-daro in nineteen twenty two under R. D. Banerji. John Marshall directed the Archaeological Survey at the time. The civilisation is called Harappan after the first site found, or Indus after the river region. Some books also call it the Indus-Saraswati civilisation.

slides.heading: Other important sites

rows: Brick basin, often called a dockyard; beads
Water reservoirs and a planned layout

visual.alt: Table of Harappan sites in India and Pakistan with what each is known for: Lothal, Kalibangan, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Chanhudaro

slides.narration: Besides the two first cities, many other sites matter. Lothal in Gujarat has a brick basin and bead workshops. Kalibangan in Rajasthan shows planned streets. Dholavira in Gujarat is known for water reservoirs. Rakhigarhi in Haryana is a large site, and Chanhudaro in Sindh was a centre of crafts.

slides.heading: Sources without a readable script
bullets: Historians depend on **archaeology**: ruins, tools, seals and sculptures.
A reading is an **interpretation** that others may test.
Say **scholars think**, not **it is certain**.

visual.alt: Flow of how historians work without a readable script: archaeologists dig and record finds, compare them with other sites, propose an interpretation, and others test it and debate
visual.caption: Reading the evidence.

slides.narration: Because the script cannot be read, historians depend on archaeology. They dig, record the finds, compare them with other sites, and propose an interpretation. Other scholars then test it and often debate it. That is why good answers use phrases such as scholars think or some historians suggest, instead of claiming certainty.

slides.narration: Many Harappan towns had two parts. The Citadel was a raised mound, usually on the western side, with important public buildings. The larger lower town to the east held the houses and workshops, laid out in blocks. The raised ground made the Citadel stand out, and some scholars think it also gave protection from floods.

slides.narration: The Great Bath was a large brick tank with steps leading down at both ends. A layer of natural tar helped make it watertight, and a corridor with rooms surrounded it. It stood on the Citadel. Many scholars think it was used for ritual bathing by the community, but that is a view, not a proven fact.

slides.heading: The granaries

rows: Brick platforms in rows near the Citadel
A large brick platform on the Citadel
Often called the great granary; some scholars question the name

visual.alt: Table of granaries: the brick platforms in rows at Harappa suggest grain storage; the large platform at Mohenjo-daro is called the great granary, though some scholars question the name

slides.narration: At Harappa, rows of raised brick platforms near the Citadel are thought to be granaries where grain was stored. At Mohenjo-daro a large brick platform on the Citadel is called the great granary, though some scholars question that name. Whatever the label, such buildings suggest that farming produced a surplus that was collected and stored.

slides.heading: The dockyard at Lothal

visual.alt: Table comparing two views of the large brick basin at Lothal: a dockyard for boats meaning sea trade was important, or a water reservoir meaning water storage mattered

slides.narration: At Lothal in Gujarat there is a large brick basin beside an old channel. Many books call it a dockyard, which would point to sea trade. Some scholars suggest it was a water reservoir instead. This difference of opinion shows why we say probable dockyard and do not state it as a certain fact.

Step 2 — State a reasonable inference.
Step 3 — Add a caution: who disagrees, or what is missing.
Step 4 — Use scholars think in the answer.

Ritual use is a view, not proof
Large brick basin by a channel

visual.alt: Table for reading three imagined finds: a tar-lined brick tank, rows of raised platforms and a basin by a channel, each with what we see, a reasonable inference and a caution

slides.narration: Here is a method for any imagined find. First describe what is visible. Then state a reasonable inference. Then add a caution. For a tar lined brick tank on a mound, we infer a public structure, and add that ritual bathing is only a view. This habit keeps answers accurate and earns full marks.

slides.heading: Seals

rows: Bull, elephant, a unicorn-like animal; a few seated figures
Pressed on clay to mark goods; found in Mesopotamia too
Some read a horned seated figure as an early god; others disagree

visual.alt: Table of seal features: made mostly of steatite, usually small and square, showing animals and a few seated figures, pressed on clay to mark goods and found in Mesopotamia; religious readings are debated

slides.narration: Seals were small, mostly square, and carved from steatite, a soft stone. They show animals such as the bull and the elephant, and a unicorn-like animal. Pressed into clay, they marked goods as belonging to a trader. Seals found in Mesopotamia show contact. One seal with a seated horned figure is read by some scholars as an early god, but others disagree.

slides.heading: The bearded man and the young woman in bronze

rows: Skill in carving; the name priest-king is a modern label
Young woman, called the dancing girl
Lost-wax casting and a lively sense of art

visual.alt: Table of two figures: the stone bearded man shows carving skill and his priest-king name is modern; the bronze young woman called the dancing girl shows lost-wax casting and lively art

slides.narration: The bearded man is a stone sculpture from Mohenjo-daro with a headband and a shawl. The name priest-king is a modern label, because no record says who he was. The bronze figure of a young woman, called the dancing girl, was made by the lost-wax method. Both show that Harappan artists were highly skilled.

slides.heading: The undeciphered script
slides.body_md: Short texts, a few hundred signs, and no key to read them.

visual.alt: Flow about the Harappan script: about 400 signs, written mostly right to left, short texts mostly on seals, undeciphered so archaeology must speak
visual.caption: What we know about the script.

slides.narration: The Harappan script has about four hundred signs and is written mostly from right to left. Most texts are short and appear on seals. Nobody has yet deciphered it, and no text in two languages has been found to help. So we cannot read about their rulers, laws or beliefs, and must depend on archaeology.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Harappa dug from **1921**, Mohenjo-daro from **1922**; mature phase **about 2600 to 1900 BCE**.
**Citadel** in the west; **Great Bath**, **granaries** and **Lothal basin** are key structures.
**Seals**, the bearded man and the bronze figure show trade, belief and art.
The **script is undeciphered**, so readings are **interpretations**.

slides.narration: In this sketch you can see house blocks, narrow lanes and a main street. In Harappan towns the roads ran north to south and east to west and crossed at right angles. Each block held several houses with courtyards. Covered drains ran along the streets. This regular layout is called a grid pattern.

slides.heading: Bricks and houses

rows: Burnt bricks in about the proportion 1 : 2 : 4
A central courtyard, a bathroom, often a well
Bins or soak pits for rubbish

visual.alt: Table of town planning features: burnt bricks in about the proportion 1 : 2 : 4, houses with a courtyard bathroom and often a well, streets crossing at right angles, and bins or soak pits for rubbish

slides.narration: Builders used burnt bricks in a standard proportion, about one to two to four for thickness, width and length. A house usually had a central courtyard with rooms around it, a bathroom, and often a well. Bins or soak pits held rubbish. Standard bricks across many towns suggest a shared way of building.

slides.heading: The covered drainage system
slides.body_md: Waste water left each house and was carried away.

visual.alt: Flow of used water: from the bathroom of a house, through a small channel in the wall, into the covered drain along the street, and carried away from the houses
visual.caption: How the drains worked.

slides.narration: Water used in a bathroom flowed through a small channel in the house wall into a covered drain along the street. The drains were roofed with bricks or stone slabs and had openings so that workers could inspect and clean them. Such a system, in a city of that age, shows high skill and care for cleanliness.

slides.body_md: Arrange the path of used water in order.

slides.heading: What does planning suggest?

visual.alt: Table of three observations with their possible meaning and a caution: grid streets suggest planning, same brick proportion suggests a common standard, covered drains suggest care for cleanliness

slides.narration: Scholars draw some inferences from the planning. Grid streets suggest that the towns were planned. The same brick proportion at distant sites suggests a common standard, and covered drains suggest care for cleanliness. But there is a caution. We cannot read any record, so we do not know who planned the towns or what rules they followed.

Read the entry, name the feature, place it under planning, craft or trade, and add a caution if the reading is uncertain. Streets at right angles and a covered drain show planning. Unfinished beads show a craft. Cubical weights show trade.

slides.heading: Internal trade

rows: Cubical stone weights in regular ratios
Beads, pottery and metals at distant towns

visual.alt: Table of evidence for internal trade: cubical stone weights in regular ratios suggest common measures, goods at distant towns suggest movement of goods, and seals pressed on clay suggest goods were marked and guarded

slides.narration: Harappans traded within their own lands. Cubical stone weights in regular ratios turn up at many sites, which suggests common measures. Beads, pottery and metals made in one place are found in other towns. Seals pressed on clay marked goods as owned and guarded them. Farmers, craftspeople and traders all depended on one another.

slides.heading: Trade with Mesopotamia
slides.body_md: Meluhha in Mesopotamian records is generally identified with the Indus region.

visual.alt: Flow of overseas trade: Harappan beads and goods travel by overseas routes to Mesopotamian cities, whose records mention Meluhha, generally identified with the Indus region
visual.caption: Trade with Mesopotamia.

slides.narration: The Harappans also traded overseas. Seals and beads in the Indus style have turned up in the cities of Mesopotamia. Mesopotamian records speak of a land called Meluhha, which is generally identified with the Indus region. Lothal, with its workshops and probable dock, may have helped this trade. Sea and land routes both seem to have been used.

slides.heading: Crafts

rows: Red clay pots with black painted designs
Baked clay animals, toys and figures

visual.alt: Table of Harappan crafts: pottery in red clay with black designs, bead-making with carnelian and other stones, metalwork in copper and bronze with no iron, terracotta figurines of baked clay, and cotton weaving

slides.narration: Harappan crafts were varied. Potters made red pots with black designs. Bead makers worked carnelian and other stones. Metalworkers used copper and bronze, but no iron has been found. Terracotta figurines of animals, toys and people were made of baked clay, and cotton was woven into cloth. Craft workshops show skilled specialist work.

slides.narration: To sort a find, first identify the material, then name the craft, and then say what the find suggests. A baked clay toy cart is a terracotta craft. Carnelian beads are bead making and may point to trade. A bronze bowl is metalwork. A red pot with black bands is pottery.

slides.heading: The decline begins
slides.body_md: From about 1900 BCE the cities shrank and were given up.

nodes.label: Signs of strain from about 1900 BCE
Cities shrink and are given up

visual.alt: Flow of decline: cities flourish, signs of strain appear from about 1900 BCE, cities shrink and are given up, and several causes are suggested
visual.caption: The story of decline.

slides.narration: From about nineteen hundred before the Common Era the great cities began to shrink, and many were given up. Why did this happen? Scholars offer several theories. None is fully proved, so each must be presented as a theory with its evidence and its limits.

slides.heading: Theories of decline

rows: Silt layers over buildings at some sites

visual.alt: Table of five theories of decline: floods, changing rivers, climate change, ecological strain and weaker trade, each with the idea and the evidence suggested

slides.narration: Here are the main theories. Floods may have damaged towns, shown by silt layers at some sites. Changing river courses, such as the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra, may have cut off water. Climate change may have reduced rainfall. Overuse of land may have strained resources, and weaker trade may have shrunk wealth. Probably several causes worked together.

slides.body_md: Towns lived by rivers; when rivers changed, towns suffered.

sections.heading: 1. Time, place and discovery
sections.body_md:
- The **Harappan** (or **Indus**) civilisation; some books add **Indus-Saraswati**. Mature phase **about 2600 to 1900 BCE**; many books teach **about 2500 to 1750 BCE**, so say **about**.
- **Harappa** (Punjab, Pakistan) dug from **1921** under **Daya Ram Sahni**; **Mohenjo-daro** (Sindh, Pakistan) from **1922** under **R. D. Banerji**; **John Marshall** was Director-General of the Archaeological Survey.
- Other sites: **Lothal** and **Dholavira** (Gujarat), **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan), **Rakhigarhi** and **Banawali** (Haryana), **Ropar** (Punjab), **Chanhudaro** (Sindh).
- Without a readable script, **archaeology** is our main source and every reading is an **interpretation**.

sections.heading: 2. The great structures
sections.body_md:
- **Citadel:** a raised mound, usually on the **western** side, with public buildings; the larger **lower town** lay to the east.
- **Great Bath** (Mohenjo-daro): a **watertight brick tank**, sealed with natural tar, with **steps** at both ends and a corridor around it. Many scholars think it was for **ritual bathing**, which is a view.
- **Granaries:** brick platforms at **Harappa**; the **great granary** of Mohenjo-daro, a name some scholars question.
- **Lothal basin** (Gujarat): often called a **dockyard**; some scholars suggest a **reservoir**.
- Each structure suggests an **organised community**, but each use is an **interpretation**.

key_terms.definition_md: The raised western mound of a Harappan town, with important public buildings.
A reading of the evidence that other scholars may test or reject.

sections.heading: 3. Seals, figures and script
sections.body_md:
- **Seals:** mostly **steatite**, usually **square**, with animals (bull, elephant, a **unicorn-like** animal) and signs; pressed on clay to **mark goods**; found in **Mesopotamia**. A seated horned figure is read by **some scholars** as an early form of a later god; others disagree.
- **Bearded man:** a stone sculpture from Mohenjo-daro; **priest-king** is a **modern label**.
- **Young woman in bronze** (dancing girl): made by **lost-wax casting**.
- **Script:** about **400 signs**, mostly **right to left**, short texts, **undeciphered**. So we cannot read of rulers, laws or beliefs.

key_terms.definition_md: A soft stone used to carve most Harappan seals.
Making a metal figure by melting away a wax model from inside a mould.
Not yet read; the Harappan script has no known key.

sections.heading: 4. Town planning
sections.body_md:
- **Grid layout:** streets ran north to south and east to west and crossed at **right angles**, dividing the town into **blocks**.
- **Burnt bricks** in about the proportion **1 : 2 : 4**; houses with a **courtyard**, a **bathroom** and often a **well**.
- **Covered drains** along the streets, roofed with bricks or slabs, with **openings** for cleaning; household channels joined them; **bins or soak pits** held rubbish.
- Scholars infer **planning** and care for cleanliness, but **who planned** is unknown.

key_terms.definition_md: A layout in which streets cross at right angles to form blocks.
A pit that lets waste water soak into the ground.

sections.heading: 5. Trade, art and craft
sections.body_md:
- **Internal trade:** goods moved between towns; **cubical stone weights** (chert) in regular ratios; **seals** marked goods.
- **External trade:** with **Mesopotamia**; Indus-style seals and beads found there; Mesopotamian records mention **Meluhha**, **generally identified** with the Indus region.
- **Crafts:** **pottery** (red with black designs), **beads** (carnelian), **metalwork** (copper and **bronze**, no **iron**), **terracotta figurines**, **cotton weaving**.
- Farmers grew crops such as wheat, barley and cotton.

key_terms.definition_md: A land named in Mesopotamian records, generally identified with the Indus region.

sections.heading: 6. Decline
sections.body_md:
- Cities shrank from **about 1900 BCE**; many were given up.
- **Theories:** **floods** (silt layers), **changing rivers** (drying of the **Ghaggar-Hakra**), **climate change** (falling rainfall), **ecological strain**, **weaker trade**.
- The **older invasion theory** blamed invaders; **most scholars now reject** it because excavations show **no clear evidence** of widespread violent destruction.
- Probably **several causes** acted together, and the effect differed from **site to site**; the unread script gives no direct record.

Damage to the land and its resources from overuse.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Stating dates without **about**, or giving one range as if every book agreed.
- Writing that the Great Bath was **certainly** for religion, or that the Lothal basin was **certainly** a dock.
- Calling the bearded man a king as a fact.
- Presenting one cause of decline as proved.
- Listing only the grid under town planning.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, term or place.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, an inference or a caution.

cards.front_md: Which two sites were dug first, and when?
cards.back_md: **Harappa** from **1921**; **Mohenjo-daro** from **1922**.

cards.front_md: Who is linked with the Harappa excavation?
cards.back_md: **Daya Ram Sahni** (from 1921).

cards.front_md: Who is linked with the Mohenjo-daro excavation?
cards.back_md: **R. D. Banerji** (from 1922).

cards.front_md: Who directed the Archaeological Survey then?
cards.back_md: **John Marshall**, as Director-General.
**About 2600 to 1900 BCE**; many books say about 2500 to 1750 BCE.

cards.front_md: Other name of the Harappan Civilisation
cards.back_md: The **Indus** civilisation (some books: Indus-Saraswati).
The **raised mound**, usually on the **western** side, with public buildings.
**Watertight brick tank**, **steps** at both ends, corridor around it; on the Citadel.

cards.front_md: Why is ritual bathing called a view?
cards.back_md: No readable record explains the Great Bath, so it is an **interpretation**.
Brick platforms for storing grain; **Harappa** and the **great granary** of Mohenjo-daro (name questioned by some scholars).
A large brick basin in **Gujarat**; many say **dockyard**, some say **reservoir**.
**Steatite**, usually **square**.
Pressed on **clay** to **mark goods**; also found in **Mesopotamia**.
Bull, elephant and a **unicorn-like** animal.
A **stone sculpture** from Mohenjo-daro; **priest-king** is a **modern label**.
A small **bronze** figure of a young woman, made by **lost-wax** casting.

cards.front_md: Why does the script limit our knowledge?
cards.back_md: **About 400 signs**, mostly right to left, **undeciphered**; we cannot read their records.
Streets crossing at **right angles**, dividing the town into **blocks**.
About **1 : 2 : 4** (thickness, width, length).
Central **courtyard**, **bathroom**, often a **well**.
House channels led into **covered street drains** with **openings** for cleaning.
Organised planning and care for cleanliness; who planned is **unknown**.
**Cubical** stone (chert) weights in **regular ratios**.
Land in Mesopotamian records, **generally identified** with the **Indus region**.
Indus-style **seals and beads** found there; **Meluhha** in the records.
Pottery, **bead-making**, metalwork, **terracotta** figurines, cotton weaving.
**Copper** and **bronze**; **no iron**.
Floods, changing rivers, climate change, ecological strain, weaker trade.
The drying of the **Ghaggar-Hakra**.
Blamed invaders; **now rejected by most scholars** (no clear evidence of widespread violence).

questions.stem_md: Excavation at Mohenjo-daro began in 1922. Which archaeologist is associated with it?

options.text_md: Daya Ram Sahni
R. D. Banerji
John Marshall, as the digger on the ground
A British engineer building a railway

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** R. D. Banerji. R. D. Banerji began the Mohenjo-daro excavation in 1922. Daya Ram Sahni is linked with Harappa, which was dug from 1921. John Marshall was Director-General of the Archaeological Survey and directed the work as a whole rather than digging at the site, and a railway engineer is not an excavator of the site.

questions.stem_md: In a large Harappan town such as Mohenjo-daro, where was the Citadel usually found?

options.text_md: On low ground on the eastern side
Inside the largest house of the lower town
Outside the town, across a river
On a raised mound on the western side of the town

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** On a raised mound on the western side of the town. The Citadel stood on a raised mound, usually on the western side, with the larger lower town spread to the east. It was not on low ground, not inside one house and not outside the town.

questions.stem_md: Which description fits the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro?

options.text_md: A large watertight brick tank with steps at both ends
A roofed hall with rows of pillars for storing grain
A brick basin joined to a channel, used to berth boats
A burial ground outside the town

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A large watertight brick tank with steps at both ends. The Great Bath was a large brick tank made watertight, with steps leading down at two ends. The hall of pillars describes a granary-like store, the basin for boats describes the Lothal structure, and it was not a burial ground.

questions.stem_md: Why do many scholars regard the Great Bath as a public structure of special importance?

options.text_md: Inscriptions on its walls state that it was a temple
It was the only building made of burnt brick in the town
Its size, careful waterproofing and place on the Citadel suggest community use, possibly ritual bathing
It was found outside the town and far from the houses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its size, careful waterproofing and place on the Citadel suggest community use, possibly ritual bathing. Scholars infer its importance from its size, its waterproofing and its position on the Citadel; the idea of ritual bathing is an interpretation. No readable inscription on it says it was a temple because the script cannot be read, burnt bricks were used all over the town, and the tank stood on the Citadel, not outside the town.

questions.stem_md: An imagined excavation diary from the mound of Sandhya Kheda records a large rectangular brick tank with steps at both ends, a layer of natural tar between the bricks and the earth, and a corridor around it, all on a raised mound. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text_md: It proves that the site was ruled by one emperor
It was certainly a granary because it is made of brick
It resembles the Great Bath, though its exact purpose, perhaps ritual bathing, remains an interpretation
It was a dockyard because it can hold water

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It resembles the Great Bath, though its exact purpose, perhaps ritual bathing, remains an interpretation. The features match the Great Bath, but a purpose such as ritual bathing is only an interpretation. The diary does not show a ruler, brick alone does not make a granary, and holding water does not make a structure a dockyard.

questions.stem_md: Many books call the large brick basin at Lothal a dockyard, but some scholars suggest it may have been a water reservoir. What does this disagreement mainly show?

options.text_md: Remains can be read in more than one way, so historians weigh evidence before concluding
Lothal had no connection with trade at all
The basin was built after the civilisation ended
Every structure at Lothal was a granary

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Remains can be read in more than one way, so historians weigh evidence before concluding. When experts differ, it shows that physical remains do not explain themselves and need careful weighing of evidence. The disagreement does not prove that Lothal lacked trade, does not date the basin, and does not make every building a granary.

questions.stem_md: At Mohenjo-daro a large brick platform on the Citadel has long been called the great granary, but some scholars question that name. Which statement reflects a careful historian's view?

options.text_md: The name must be correct because it appears in many books
It must have been a palace because it stands on the Citadel
Since it cannot be proved, the platform never existed
The name is an interpretation, and storage remains are needed to support it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The name is an interpretation, and storage remains are needed to support it. A label is an interpretation until evidence supports it, so historians look for storage remains. Repetition in books is not proof, a palace is also only a guess, and a doubtful name does not make the physical platform disappear.

questions.stem_md: The raised mound that held important buildings in Harappan towns is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: It is called the Citadel and was usually on the western side of the town.

questions.stem_md: The large brick basin at Lothal in Gujarat is described by many scholars as a ___.
questions.solution_md: Many scholars call it a dockyard, although some suggest other uses.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Scholars have proved from written records that the Great Bath was used only for religious bathing.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** No written record that we can read explains the Great Bath. Ritual bathing is a view held by many scholars, not a proven fact.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro is regarded as a public structure.

**Reason (R):** It stood in the lower town among the ordinary houses.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: its size and care suggest community use. R is false: it stood on the Citadel, not in the lower town.

questions.stem_md: What was the Citadel of a Harappan town, and where was it usually placed?
questions.solution_md: Meaning and position.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Citadel** was a **raised mound** that carried important public buildings, such as the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro. It was usually on the **western side** of the town, above the larger lower town.

marking_scheme.step: Western side, above the lower town

questions.stem_md: An imagined museum model labelled the Citadel of Mohenjo-daro shows a large brick tank with a corridor around it. State two more features that would let a visitor identify it as the Great Bath.
questions.solution_md: Any two features.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It was a large **brick tank** made **watertight** with a lining of natural tar.
2. It had **steps** at both ends and a **corridor** around it, and stood on the **Citadel**.

questions.stem_md: Why do historians speak of the Lothal basin as a probable dockyard rather than a certain one?
questions.solution_md: Two readings, therefore an interpretation.

answer.model_answer_md: Some scholars read the brick basin as a **dock** linked to sea trade, but others suggest a **water reservoir**. Since no readable record explains it, the use is an **interpretation** that must be weighed.

marking_scheme.step: No readable record, so an interpretation

questions.stem_md: Name three important structures of the Harappan Civilisation and state what each tells us.
questions.solution_md: Three structures, each linked to what it shows.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Great Bath** suggests skill in brick building and perhaps shared **ritual bathing**.
2. The **granaries** suggest that **grain** was collected and stored.
3. The **dockyard at Lothal**, if it was one, suggests **sea trade**; some scholars question this.

questions.stem_md: A team digging the imagined mound of Karnai finds a large brick basin beside a dry channel. Give two reasons it may be a dock and one reason for caution.
questions.solution_md: Two supporting reasons and one caution.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Its **size** and brick lining resemble the **Lothal** basin that many call a dockyard.
2. It lies beside a **channel** that boats may once have used.
3. **Caution:** it could also be a **reservoir**, and no readable record names its purpose.

questions.stem_md: Most Harappan seals were carved from which material?

options.text_md: Iron
Steatite, a soft stone
Glass
Marble

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Steatite, a soft stone. Most seals were carved from steatite, a soft stone that is easy to cut and polish. Iron was not used by the Harappans, glass is not the usual material and marble is not typical.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Harappan town, a trader presses a small square seal into a lump of clay that holds a bundle of goods shut. What would this most likely achieve?

options.text_md: It would mark the bundle as his and show it had not been opened
It would record the price in a script we can read today
It would pay the town's tax to a ruler
It would write the date of the journey

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It would mark the bundle as his and show it had not been opened. Seals were pressed into clay to mark ownership and to guard goods, which is why they are linked with trade. The signs cannot be read today, so a readable price is not the reason; taxes and dates are not shown by this use.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Mesopotamian city of Urnashar, excavators find a small square seal showing an animal and signs in the Indus style. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text_md: Mesopotamians invented the Harappan script
There was contact, probably trade, between Mesopotamia and the Indus region
Harappan armies once ruled Urnashar
The two regions spoke exactly the same language

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** There was contact, probably trade, between Mesopotamia and the Indus region. An Indus-style seal found far away points to contact, most probably trade. It does not show who invented the script, any conquest, or a shared language.

questions.stem_md: One seal shows a seated figure with a horned headdress, surrounded by animals. Some scholars see an early form of a later god; others disagree. How should a student treat this reading?

options.text_md: As proof that the Harappans worshipped a god known later
As proof that the Harappans had no religion
As one possible interpretation that cannot be confirmed while the script is unread
As a map of the city

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** As one possible interpretation that cannot be confirmed while the script is unread. The reading is an interpretation: since the script cannot be read, no text confirms it. It is not proof of later worship, it does not show an absence of religion, and the picture is not a map.

questions.stem_md: A stone sculpture of a bearded man, found at Mohenjo-daro, is often called the priest-king. Why do careful historians say this label is modern?

options.text_md: The sculpture itself was made in modern times
It shows a king of a later dynasty
The script on it names him as a priest
No readable record says who he was; the name was given by modern scholars as a guess

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** No readable record says who he was; the name was given by modern scholars as a guess. Nobody can read a Harappan text that names him, so the title is a modern guess. The sculpture is ancient, it is not from a later dynasty, and the script cannot be read.

questions.stem_md: The small bronze figure of a young woman from Mohenjo-daro, popularly called the dancing girl, is valued by historians mainly because it shows

options.text_md: that the Harappans used iron weapons
that every woman danced in temples
the readable name of the artist
skill in metal casting by the lost-wax method and a lively sense of art

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** skill in metal casting by the lost-wax method and a lively sense of art. The figure shows the Harappans could cast bronze by the lost-wax method and could model a graceful figure. It does not show iron, a custom of temple dancing, or a name, because the script cannot be read.

questions.stem_md: In which direction were most Harappan inscriptions written?

options.text_md: Always from left to right
From top to bottom in one column
Mostly from right to left
In a spiral from the centre

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Mostly from right to left. Most inscriptions seem to run from right to left. They are not always left to right, in single downward columns, or in spirals.

questions.stem_md: Which statement explains why the script limits what we know about the Harappans?

options.text_md: It has only five signs and says very little
It has not been deciphered, so we cannot read what they wrote about rulers, beliefs or laws
It was copied from Mesopotamian writing and adds nothing new
It has been fully read, but the records were lost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It has not been deciphered, so we cannot read what they wrote about rulers, beliefs or laws. The script, with about four hundred signs, is still undeciphered, so we must depend mainly on archaeology. It does not have only five signs, it was not copied from Mesopotamia, and it has not been fully read.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Ratnapur Herald reports the discovery of the longest known Harappan inscription, of forty signs, and a student says it will at once reveal the names of Harappan kings. Which reply is most accurate?

options.text_md: A longer text helps study sign patterns, but it cannot be read until the script is deciphered
Correct, because every inscription gives names
Wrong, because the Harappans had no writing at all
Wrong, because inscriptions appear only on pottery

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A longer text helps study sign patterns, but it cannot be read until the script is deciphered. More text gives scholars more patterns to study, but without a decipherment, or a bilingual text, it cannot be read. The Harappans did have writing, and inscriptions appear on seals as well as other objects.

questions.stem_md: The Harappan script has about 400 signs and is still ___, so we depend largely on archaeology.
questions.solution_md: It is undeciphered, so no one can yet read what it says.

questions.stem_md: The bronze figure of the young woman from Mohenjo-daro was made by the ___ method of casting.
questions.solution_md: The figure was cast by the lost-wax method.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Written records tell us for certain that the bearded stone figure from Mohenjo-daro was a priest-king.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** No readable record names him. Priest-king is a modern label given by scholars as a guess.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Scholars have fully understood the messages on Harappan seals.

**Reason (R):** The Harappan script, with about 400 signs, has not been deciphered.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the seals cannot be read. R is true: the script is undeciphered.

questions.stem_md: Match each Harappan source with what it is thought to show.

options.text_md: Great Bath
Basin at Lothal
Steatite seals
Bronze figure of a young woman

match_right.text_md: A probable dockyard linked to sea trade
Metal casting by the lost-wax method
A watertight brick tank, possibly for ritual bathing
Stamps with animals and signs, used in trade

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The Great Bath is a tank, the Lothal basin a probable dockyard, seals were stamps used in trade, and the bronze figure shows lost-wax casting.

questions.stem_md: Excavators at the imagined mound of Dholakot find a clay lump bearing the impression of a square steatite seal with an animal. State two things historians can learn from seals like it.
questions.solution_md: Any two points.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Seals pressed on clay show that **trade** was carefully organised, since goods were marked.
2. Their animal figures and scenes give hints about **religious beliefs**, and seals found in Mesopotamia show **overseas contact**.

questions.stem_md: A notice at the imagined Lokmanya School claims that Class IX has read a Harappan seal and found the name of a king. Give two reasons why a historian would be cautious.
questions.solution_md: Undeciphered, so claims need proof.

answer.model_answer_md: The script, with about **400 signs**, has **not been deciphered**, so no one can read a seal and name a king. Scholars must depend on **archaeological remains**, whose meaning is often **debated**, so such a claim needs strong proof.

marking_scheme.step: Script not deciphered, so nothing can be read
Reliance on debated remains; claim needs proof

questions.stem_md: Describe the bearded man sculpture of Mohenjo-daro and say why the name priest-king is only a modern label.
questions.solution_md: Description and the reason for caution.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a **stone sculpture** of a **bearded man** with a headband and a shawl over one shoulder. The name **priest-king** was given by **modern scholars**; no readable record tells who he was.

marking_scheme.step: Modern label, no record of identity

questions.stem_md: Explain the importance of Harappan seals as a source of information on trade and religion.
questions.solution_md: Trade, overseas contact and religion with caution.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Seals were pressed into **clay** on goods, which shows **trade** and the marking of ownership.
2. Seals found in **Mesopotamia** show **contact** with distant lands.
3. Animals and a seated figure on some seals hint at **religious ideas**, but such readings are **interpretations** because the script is unread.

questions.stem_md: Describe the bearded man and the dancing girl and say what each reveals about Harappan art.
questions.solution_md: Each figure described, with what it reveals.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **bearded man** is a carved **stone sculpture** with a shawl, showing skill in carving.
2. The **dancing girl** is a small **bronze** figure of a young woman, showing the **lost-wax** casting method.
3. Together they show that Harappan artists could model the **human figure** with skill.

marking_scheme.step: Bearded man with what it shows
Bronze figure with what it shows

questions.stem_md: A model-maker at the imagined Rajtilak Museum must build a Harappan town in miniature, and wants the streets to match the real pattern. Which layout should she choose?

options.text_md: Winding lanes with no plan
Streets that cross at right angles and divide the town into blocks
One circular road around the town
Scattered houses without any roads

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Streets that cross at right angles and divide the town into blocks. Harappan streets crossed one another at right angles to form a grid of blocks. The other layouts are unplanned or circular and do not match the evidence.

questions.stem_md: A model-maker at the imagined Rajtilak Museum casts miniature bricks that are 5 cm thick and wants them to keep the usual Harappan proportion of thickness, width and length. How long should each brick be?

options.text_md: 10 cm
15 cm
45 cm
20 cm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 20 cm. The usual proportion is about 1 : 2 : 4, so a thickness of 5 cm gives a width of about 10 cm and a length of about 20 cm. A length of 10 cm would be the width, 15 cm fits no ratio and 45 cm follows a 1 : 3 : 9 pattern.

questions.stem_md: An imagined excavator at Kothari Mound uncovers a street drain roofed with brick slabs, with openings at intervals. What was the most likely purpose of the openings?

options.text_md: To allow the drain to be inspected and cleaned
To let boats enter the town
To store grain safely
To pour religious offerings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** To allow the drain to be inspected and cleaned. Openings in a covered drain allow workers to inspect and clear blockages, as in other Harappan drains. Boats, grain storage and offerings have no link with a roofed drain.

questions.stem_md: Some historians argue that a regular grid and standard bricks suggest planning by an organised authority. Which caution should a student add?

options.text_md: Only foreign architects could have planned such towns
Grids are found only in modern cities
We cannot read Harappan records, so the nature of that authority remains uncertain
A planned town never needs any authority

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** We cannot read Harappan records, so the nature of that authority remains uncertain. With the script unread, nothing tells us who planned the towns or how, so the claim stays an inference. The other options contradict the evidence or are simply untrue.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the path of used water in a Harappan town in the correct order.

options.text_md: Is carried along the drain away from the houses
Used in the bathroom of a house
Enters the covered drain running along the street
Flows through a small channel in the house wall

questions.stem_md:

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Great Bath** was a large **brick tank** made **watertight** with a lining of natural tar. It had **steps** at both ends and a corridor around it, and stood on the **Citadel**.

(ii) The **Citadel** was a **raised mound**, usually on the western side, carrying important public buildings. The **granaries**, such as those at Harappa, suggest that **grain** was collected and stored by an organised community.

(iii) The Great Bath suggests skill in building and possibly **ritual bathing**; the Citadel suggests a **planned centre**; granaries suggest **farming surplus** and storage. Historians must be careful: the script is **unread**, so uses such as bathing or the name **great granary** are **interpretations**, and some scholars question them.

questions.stem_md:
Seals and sculptures help us to imagine the Harappans.

(i) Describe Harappan seals: their material, shape and common figures. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the bearded man and the dancing girl. **[3]**
(iii) Explain why the undeciphered script limits our knowledge of the Harappans. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Seals; the two figures; limits of the script.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Most seals were carved from **steatite**, a soft stone, and were usually **square**. They show animals such as the **bull**, the elephant and a **unicorn-like** animal, along with a few signs.

(ii) The **bearded man** is a stone sculpture with a headband and shawl; the name **priest-king** is a modern label. The **dancing girl** is a small **bronze** figure of a young woman, made by **lost-wax** casting.

(iii) The script has about **400 signs**, is written mostly **right to left**, and is **undeciphered**. So we cannot read about **rulers, laws, beliefs or history**. We must depend on **archaeology**, whose finds, like the seal of a seated figure, can be read in **more than one way**.

questions.stem_md:

(i) Describe the grid layout of the streets. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the bricks and houses of the towns. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the drainage system and say what it suggests about the people. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Grid; bricks and houses; drainage and what it suggests.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Streets ran **north to south and east to west** and crossed at **right angles**, dividing the town into **blocks**. The main streets were wide, and narrow lanes ran between the houses.

(ii) Houses were built of **burnt bricks** of a standard proportion, about **1 : 2 : 4**. Many had a central **courtyard**, a **bathroom** and a **well**, and rooms opened on the courtyard.

(iii) Waste water ran from house bathrooms into **covered drains** along the streets, with **openings** for cleaning, and **bins or soak pits** held waste. This suggests **care for cleanliness**, **skilled engineering** and an **organised authority**, although what kind of authority is unknown.

questions.stem_md:
The Harappans were skilled traders and craftspeople.

(i) Describe their internal trade and weights. **[3]**
(ii) Describe their external trade, especially with Mesopotamia. **[3]**

questions.solution_md: Internal trade; Mesopotamia; four crafts.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Goods such as **grain, beads, pottery and metals** moved between towns and villages, and **seals** pressed on clay marked goods as owned. **Cubical weights**, made of stone such as chert, were found in regular ratios at many sites, which suggests **common measures** in exchange.

(ii) The Harappans traded overseas, above all with **Mesopotamia**. **Indus-style seals and beads** have been found there, and Mesopotamian records speak of **Meluhha**, generally identified with the **Indus region**.

(iii) **Pottery**: red pots with black painted designs. **Bead-making**: carnelian and other stones. **Metalwork**: copper and bronze, but no iron has been found. **Terracotta figurines**: baked clay animals, toys and figures. (Also **cotton weaving**, using cotton grown locally.)

questions.stem_md:
The Harappan cities declined after about 1900 BCE.

(i) State three theories that have been put forward for the decline. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how changing rivers and climate change could have weakened the cities. **[3]**
(iii) Why do most scholars today reject the older invasion theory, and why is no single explanation accepted by all? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Three theories; mechanism; rejection of invasion and no single cause.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Floods**, **changes in river courses** such as the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra, and **climate change** with falling rainfall. (Also **ecological strain** and **weaker trade**.)

(ii) Farming and towns depended on **rivers and rain**. If a river **shifted or dried**, or rainfall **fell**, harvests shrank, towns lost their **water and food**, and people **moved away**.

(iii) An older theory blamed **invaders**, but excavations show **no clear evidence** of widespread violent destruction, and decline looks **gradual**. No single cause is accepted because the **area was vast**, evidence **differs between sites** and the script is **unread**, so scholars see **several causes** working together.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Effect of drying or less rain
(iii) Why the invasion theory is rejected

children.stem_md: What may the layer of silt point to?

answer.model_answer_md: A **flood**.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain why the second team member is cautious.

answer.model_answer_md: Towns declined at **different times**, so one cause cannot be applied to all of them. More **evidence** from other sites is needed before **firm conclusions** can be drawn.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): State two other theories of decline that the report does not name.

answer.model_answer_md: An **older theory blamed invaders**, which most scholars now reject. Others suggest **ecological strain** from overusing land, or **weaker trade** with distant lands.
